statements.text: So, I appreciate some of the ideas that have been put forth, but one of the things that has intrigued me and I think it probably intrigues a lot of people, and this is in the few moments that I have left in the committee today, is the use of artificial intelligence in some of this and trying to find the fraud.
statements.context: House Oversight Committee hearing on waste, fraud, and abuse in federal pandemic spending.

statements.text: But the development of AI, how will that impact our inter- national relations specifically with China? I fear what they will do if they get control of it, as you have stated there.
statements.context: House Oversight Committee hearing titled "Advances in AI: Are We Ready For a Tech Revolution?" on March 8, 2023.

statements.text: I’m definitely not an expert in AI, but I would like to talk about the fears and concerns that people in my district and people all over the country have when it comes to AI. We certainly don’t like the idea of AI replacing humans and re- placing people, especially when it comes to jobs.
statements.context: House hearing titled "Advances in AI: Are We Ready For a Tech Revolution?" where Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene questions witnesses about AI risks.

statements.text: we've talked about algorithms for years, like on social media, and the use of divisiveness of politics today, and each side getting the extreme of their side and getting fed more of that information. I sort of feel like it would be—we were putting it on steroids of the future, immediate future of what the advances in AI might be.
statements.context: Question posed during a House Oversight Committee hearing titled "Advances in AI: Are We Ready for a Tech Revolution?"

statements.text: I don't think that we are ready for what is going to happen in a very short period of time. And I think, if it is not happening already, it will be in the next five years where AI will be programming AI, and then what's next?
statements.context: Closing remarks by the subcommittee chair at a House oversight hearing on AI readiness.

statements.text: do we need to be worried about too much advancement too fast in AI? Are we capable of developing AI that could pose a danger to humanity's existence all over the world, some of the things that people talk about out of fear in this conversation because of a lack of knowledge, or is that just science fiction?
statements.context: House hearing titled 'Advances in AI: Are We Ready for a Tech Revolution?', where Rep. Mace questions an expert witness.

statements.text: To achieve this, we need to establish guidelines for AI development and use. [...] We need to establish a clear legal framework to hold companies accountable for the consequences of their AI systems.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Nancy Mace (Subcommittee Chair) at a House Oversight subcommittee hearing on AI, later revealed to have been generated by ChatGPT.

statements.text: How can we ensure that AI technology is developed in a way that is safe, transparent, and beneficial for society without stifling innovation?
statements.context: Opening questions by Rep. Mace at the House's first AI hearing of the Congress.

statements.text: Congress is grappling with technology. Our country’s grappling with technology. And we’re doing our best to try to figure out a reg- ulatory environment that fosters innovation and allows economic growth, while managing the potential adverse impacts that tech- nology can have.
statements.context: House hearing titled "Advances in AI: Are We Ready For a Tech Revolution?"; the speaker is questioning a witness panel.

statements.text: But I have great concerns just at what some of our vulnerabilities may be both from a defensive and offensive side of things.
statements.context: House Armed Services Committee hearing on U.S. Special Operations Forces challenges and resource priorities for FY2024.

statements.text: Artificial intelligence and what it brings in terms of the applications, first and foremost, for us is about putting those applications over oceans of data that we have in the Department, [...] and using those applications to crush that information, synthesize it for us, and get it to us with speed.
statements.context: House Armed Services Committee hearing on U.S. Special Operations Forces challenges and resource priorities for FY2024.

statements.text: In particular, I am going back to AI, everything that I come back to, because it is advancing so quickly. [...] We just do not know what we do not know, and we do not know how it will impact us, the vulnerabilities that we have. [...] We will be putting out a portfolio of legislation to be helpful [...]
statements.context: Closing remarks by Rep. Mace at a House Oversight subcommittee hearing on the White House National Cybersecurity Strategy, addressed to the witness.

statements.text: Our first hearing was on AI in this committee, and there are things that we cannot even imagine how AI will be used. I read a story the other day about ChatGPT getting through CAPTCHA, like, with a TaskRabbit employee, and told them that they were visually impaired, to break into that. [...] How are we going to use some of these tools to ensure that we defend ourselves against breaches that we cannot even be aware of right now?
statements.context: Rep. Mace questions a witness about AI's role in the White House National Cybersecurity Strategy during a House subcommittee hearing.

statements.text: And also the investments that we are making, we are looking to invest $1.8 billion into AI.
statements.context: House Armed Services Committee hearing on the FY2024 defense budget request, with questions to Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin and General Mark Milley.

statements.text: It is essential we adopt and deploy this new technology responsibly and faster than our adversaries in order to maintain operational and decision advantage. [...] It is also imperative that we continue to integrate Allies and partners in the development and delivery of AI to facilitate building a modern infrastructure capable of supporting AI applications.
statements.context: Written testimony from General Cavoli submitted to the House Armed Services Committee in response to a question from Rep. Mace about AI and emerging technologies in the USEUCOM theatre.

statements.text: We are clearly at a turning point in the role Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays on the battlefield. The Ukrainian Armed Forces have incorporated new technology and AI applications with incredible speed and agility. They have employed AI applications to enhance battlefield intelligence and to improve weapons and tactics against Russian forces.
statements.context: General Cavoli, Commander of U.S. European Command, testifies before Congress on military posture and national security challenges in Europe.

statements.text: there have been a lot of concerns about AI and technologies, robotics, et cetera. There are some people that would see the robot dog, as I am going to call it, and think that that might be utilized, you know, years from now, not any time soon, against them. [...] in thinking about some of the concerns, whether it is data security, cybersecurity, you know, the advent of AI is moving technology and cybersecurity threats in rapid pace. [...] how do we prepare ourselves for that future. What are your concerns? How are we addressing those concerns, et cetera?
statements.context: House committee hearing on using cutting-edge technologies for national security, during a Q&A with panelists.

statements.text: And I have a message for Elon Musk today: We are not going to pause AI development or research or innovation for six months because China is not going to pause its research or its AI development at any time or any moment in the near or distant future.
statements.context: Opening statement by the Subcommittee chair at a congressional hearing on cutting-edge security technologies, including AI applications for border security and defense.

statements.text: In talking about AI and currently the role AI plays on your company's unmanned drones and unmanned ground robots, et cetera, what sort of role does AI play? How do you anticipate AI now and in the future playing a larger role in these types of technologies?
statements.context: Congresswoman Nancy Mace questioning a witness during a House Subcommittee hearing on cutting-edge technologies and national security.

statements.text: Recent developments in AI will change the way we live and work, and we must maintain our edge over China in AI development. [...] The capabilities of robots, drones, scanners and other security hardware may be supercharged by advances in AI, and we have seen some of those advances today.
statements.context: Closing remarks by the Subcommittee Chair at the end of a hearing on using cutting-edge technologies for national security.

statements.text: but also the existential risks, to quote him, as well.
statements.context: House Oversight Committee business meeting marking up the AI Training Expansion Act, a bipartisan bill to expand AI training for Federal employees.

statements.text: AI can make government work better, but it is still just a tool, be it an incredibly powerful one, and like any tool, can easily be abused when used for the wrong purposes or without the proper guardrails.
statements.context: Opening statement by the subcommittee chair at a congressional oversight hearing on federal AI use.

statements.text: We are working today in the White House on an executive order. The Office of Management and Budget is work- ing on guidance for departments and agencies.
statements.context: House Oversight Subcommittee hearing on federal agency AI adoption; Dr. Martell, DOD Chief Digital and AI Officer, delivers his opening statement.

statements.text: OMB is more than 2 years late in complying with a congressional mandate to give Federal agencies guidance on the acquisition and use of AI. [...] Why is the process stalled? When can we expect to see some guidance?
statements.context: House Oversight Committee hearing on federal AI use, during a time-limited final round of questioning.

statements.text: That inventory has been appropriately criticized in the press as being inconsistent and incomplete. The inventory is lacking uniformity, and some significant AI use cases have been omitted. So, is your office doing anything to improve the inventories, to improve transparency with the public? What does that look like?
statements.context: House Oversight Committee hearing on federal agency AI use, where Rep. Mace questions a witness about the quality of agency AI inventories.

statements.text: Do we have defenses, or what kind of defenses do we have against AI-powered attacks?
statements.context: Rep. Mace poses the question during a House hearing on combating ransomware attacks.

statements.text: The groundbreaking power of artificial intelligence is a double-edged sword. [...] The latest AI algorithms can be used to make synthetic creations nearly indistinguishable from actual faces, voices, and events. These creations are referred to as deepfakes. [...] deepfake technology can also be weaponized and cause great harm. It can be used to make people appear to say or do things that they have not said or done. It can be used to perpetuate various crimes, including financial fraud and intellectual property theft. It can also be used by anti-American actors to create national security threats, and these are not hypothetical harms.
statements.context: Opening statement by the subcommittee chair at a hearing on advances in deepfake technology in the U.S. House of Representatives.

statements.text: I would say, though, that even if we have disclosure in terms of deepfakes, this targeting of women who are political figures, even if it is satire, I think that it is a problem and something that we really need to hone in on.
statements.context: House Oversight Committee hearing on "Advances in Deepfake Technology," during the questioning portion led by Rep. Connolly.

statements.text: I would like to ask a question of Dr. Ho. You have written about the lack of AI talent in government and the failure of this Administration to timely implement AI-related mandates. [...] So, under this new EO, it has got 150 new tasks to perform based on your count. Do you expect Federal agencies to meet the timetables for actions set out in the EO?
statements.context: Congressional hearing in which Rep. Mace questions a witness about federal capacity to implement a recent AI executive order.

statements.text: The biggest risk concerning government use of AI is that it will not happen fast enough, like everything. I mean, today we still have legacy systems throughout the Federal Government, and we are all asking ourselves why. [...] So, could slow and reluctant government adoption of AI jeopardize the cybersecurity of Federal systems? Is this a national security issue? Where do you see it?
statements.context: Congresswoman Nancy Mace questioning a witness during a congressional hearing on White House AI policy.

statements.text: You cannot create bioweapons as it is today. Why would AI be any different? AI obviously could not be helpful in that either.
statements.context: Closing remarks by Rep. Mace at a congressional hearing on White House AI policy.

statements.text: Since the release of ChatGPT just over a year ago, it has become clear AI could soon disrupt nearly every facet of our economy and society from healthcare to warfare. And that is good news. AI is a triumph of American innovation. [...] But like any powerful tool, AI could be used to inflict great harm when it is used carelessly or by malicious actors. That is why we have explored the dark side of AI in this Subcommittee, the risk that AI-fueled cyber-attacks pose to our national security and critical infrastructure, the threats to data privacy, the ways child sexual abuse material can proliferate online via deepfake technology, and the risk of personal harm to individuals from unchecked algorithmic bias.
statements.context: Opening statement by the subcommittee chair at a House Oversight Subcommittee on Cybersecurity hearing on the Biden AI executive order and OMB AI guidance.

statements.text: By farming out so many decisions to individual agencies, are either of you worried about the EO and the guidance might lead to multiple, conflicting, AI-enforcement regimes within the government?
statements.context: Q&A panel discussion on White House AI policy, likely a congressional or think-tank event, with questions directed to Brian Nodurft and a Ms. Goodloe.

statements.text: We need a Khan Academy of AI is what we need. [...] Are you saying that the terms of the Federal contracts IBM is asked to sign prohibit the work be done by those without college degrees? Does that inhibit your ability to fill those roles?
statements.context: House hearing titled "Toward an AI-Ready Workforce" chaired by Rep. Nancy Mace.

statements.text: Your testimony states that robust implementation of the AI and Government Act by the executive branch would be a key first step in preparing the Federal workforce for a new way to work using AI. [...] OPM has done none of that. How can Congress ensure the Federal workforce is AI ready if we do not know the current skill level in agencies or their future needs?
statements.context: Rep. Mace questions a witness at a House Oversight Subcommittee hearing on preparing the Federal workforce for AI.

statements.text: One of our big challenges in the digital revolution, combined with the AI revolution, is how we avoid the growing disparity in income that we have seen so far and disparity of opportunity.
statements.context: House hearing titled 'Toward an AI-Ready Workforce'; Rep. Khanna questions an expert panel on closing the digital opportunity gap.

statements.text: I think it is really important to think about AI is going to change 90 percent of jobs, right? So, we need to think about how, one of the Members mentioned, around freeing people up from redundant tasks that you may not want, that is not the most exciting part of our work. [...] I absolutely acknowledge the uncertainty, but if we have transparency about more jobs that are being created, jobs are being elevated in our H.R. function.
statements.context: House hearing on AI workforce readiness, with Representative Burlison questioning witnesses about AI-related job transformation and reskilling.

statements.text: Today, America is indisputably the global leader in artificial intelligence, which is why you all are here today. This Nation has led the way on AI.
statements.context: Opening statement by the Subcommittee Chair at a congressional hearing on AI workforce readiness.

statements.text: But I filed a bill with some of my colleagues last week that would take deepfakes, if they are in the likeness of a real person, and make it a crime.
statements.context: Opening statement by the subcommittee chair at a House hearing on deepfake harms.

statements.text: OK. Thank you. According to the executive order, the over 100-page executive order, irresponsible use of AI could exacer- bate ‘‘social harms,’’ including, ‘‘disinformation.’’ Should we trust the government to be the ultimate arbiter of what is disinformation and what may cause social harm in AI systems? [...] we should be concerned about the First Amendment approach of doing such.
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing titled 'White House Overreach on AI,' with the chair questioning a witness about the Biden AI executive order.

statements.text: But this executive order does so anyway and invokes the emergency powers of the Defense Production Act, or DPA, to require AI developers to notify the government if they are even considering developing new AI systems. [...] It also mandates they regularly hand over highly sensitive proprietary data, like testing results, to the Commerce Department.
statements.context: Opening statement by the subcommittee chair at a House Oversight subcommittee hearing examining the Biden administration's AI executive order.

statements.text: We want to make sure that the United States is the clear winner, the clear innovator in all technology, including AI. We do not want to stifle innovation. We do not want to stifle investment in AI or its innovation in any way, shape, or form. There is a lot at risk here, and we do not want our adversaries getting ahead of us or giving them the room or the rope to get ahead of us at all, so thank you again.
statements.context: Closing remarks by the Subcommittee chair at a congressional hearing on AI oversight and innovation.

statements.text: The executive order is actually one of the longest EOs ever written at over 100 pages, and it absolutely will encumber tech in a lot of ways, as we heard from our witnesses this morning. [...] the Commerce Department could not protect Secretary Raimondo's own email account from being hacked last year, yet this EO requires firms to share with the Agency on a daily basis the crown jewel secrets of the most powerful AI systems on earth.
statements.context: House Oversight Committee hearing titled 'White House Overreach on AI,' where Rep. Mace questions a witness panel about the Biden AI executive order.

statements.text: How does this EO stifle innovation, limit potentially investments in AI in the United States?
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing titled 'White House Overreach on AI,' where Chairwoman Mace questions a panel of experts about the impact of the Biden AI executive order on innovation and investment.

statements.text: They do not have to follow U.S. law or regulation. [...] I just would like to add, I think the example you provided shows why it is so difficult to define AI, and why one of the concerns that I know Mr. Chilson expressed about the defini- tions in the executive order that could reach very far into everyday algorithms or everyday technologies that we are using can be con- cerning, is in the defense context, we often hear that mentioned as a high-risk scenario.
statements.context: Congressional hearing titled 'White House Overreach on AI,' where Ms. Mace chairs and questions witnesses about regulatory approaches to AI.

statements.text: The EO requires companies even considering developing dual use foundation AI models to report to the government on an ongoing basis again about their most sensitive business secrets. [...] Could the justification for using the DPA here be used in the future to demand highly sensitive plans and data from firms in any emerging technology field?
statements.context: House Oversight Committee hearing titled 'White House Overreach on AI,' where Rep. Mace questions witnesses about executive-order reporting requirements.

statements.text: I would never, ever, ever, ever want to see government regulation, government requirements stifle our ability for this American company to advance technology as fast as it has.
statements.context: House Oversight Committee hearing on AI regulation, where Rep. Mace questions witnesses about balancing AI innovation with national security competitiveness.

statements.text: Should AI model developers have to give the government all their test results and test data, even those concerning politics or religion?
statements.context: Congressional hearing titled 'White House Overreach on AI' where Ms. Mace questions a witness.

statements.text: OK. AI and quantum computing are powerful new tools in the arsenal of both hackers and defenders in cyberspace. How much does defense of critical U.S. computer systems hinge on our ability to maintain and buildupon our edge in AI over China?
statements.context: Question posed during a House hearing on cyber threats from China.

statements.text: the advances in AI and technology, the amount of energy that is needed and going to be needed in the near future to keep up with the advances in how fast things are going. The data centers. Is it nuclear? What is it? How do we handle what is going to come in terms of—in order to keep up with the technology we have got to have the energy capability, the energy infrastructure. We have to have the data centers to be able to keep up.
statements.context: House Armed Services Committee hearing on DOD technology acquisition, where Rep. Mace questions industry witnesses about chips, energy, and data-center needs for AI.

statements.text: These concerns must always be at the forefront of any conversation on the use of technology, and especially artificial intelligence, across Federal Government.
statements.context: Opening remarks at a House subcommittee hearing on leveraging technology to strengthen immigration enforcement.

statements.text: The advent of AI and what it can be used, bigger, better, faster, more safer, more secure, just comments on—I just—we have so much money the government can spend. There is just so much opportunity here to invest in high-speed tech that can help us. Why are we not using AI to make it all better, faster, more?
statements.context: Rep. Nancy Mace asks a witness about using AI for government efficiency during a House oversight hearing on IT modernization.

statements.text: AI is no longer some futuristic idea. It is here and it is already reshaping everything from health care and national defense to finance and fraud prevention.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Nancy Mace (Chair of the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation) at a House Oversight Committee hearing on the federal government's use of AI.

statements.text: One of my concerns, coming from a technology background [...] the Federal Government has real challenges with moving forward in a quick way and competing against our adversaries. [...] if you could just do one thing today to help us utilize AI and technology to move the ball forward, what is that?
statements.context: Congresswoman Nancy Mace opens her questioning period at a hearing on the Federal Government in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.

statements.text: What do you think it will take to get there, where AI is creating its own AI?
statements.context: Congresswoman Nancy Mace poses a question to a witness at a House hearing on the future of artificial intelligence.

statements.text: What are the consequences—and this is for all the panelists—if the United States fails to outpace China in the race for domination in AI?
statements.context: Question posed by Rep. Mace to a panel at a congressional hearing on the future of artificial intelligence.

statements.text: Some experts warn we are just a few years away from the emergence of artificial general intelligence or the singularity. Others argue that technology has inherent limitations, and we are decades away from the singularity, if it is even possible.
statements.context: Opening statement by the chairwoman at a House subcommittee hearing on the future of artificial intelligence.

statements.text: But I do want to talk to you about the future of AI. Elon Musk has said that, as early as 2026, we would have singularity, basically. Define singularity, and how quickly do you think we are going to get there?
statements.context: Rep. Mace poses the question during a hearing titled 'Shaping Tomorrow: The Future of Artificial Intelligence.'
